site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Narada's Gentle Lesson
body: At a grand sacrifice, the learned Brahmins grew proud of their scholarship, turning away every visitor who came to the holy gathering. When the young sage Narada arrived, they brushed him aside as a wandering singer and refused to honor him at the fire.

Narada only smiled and softly hummed a single verse, singing that the vain shrink while the humble grow. Listening, the priests felt their hearts quietly open, and the pride that had hardened them began to melt like morning mist.
Bowing their heads before Narada, the Brahmins asked him to teach them, and the sacrifice ended as it should have begun, with a warm feast shared freely among all who had come.

stories.title: The Little Dove's Wisdom
stories.source: Panchatantra · Tantra 3 (Crows and Owls), 'The Self-Sacrificing Dove' — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: In an Indian forest clearing, a hunter spread his net and scattered grain to lure birds. One small dove swooped down alone, then stopped before a single peck. "Do not linger," she told the hunter gently, "for this very net will surely catch you." The man stared, astonished that a creature so small could warn him.

"How could a bird like you possibly harm me?" he asked, half-laughing. The dove tilted her head and replied that the wise perceive danger long before it arrives, and so they choose to act now while they still can. Her quiet certainty made him pause, the morning birdsong softening around them.

Something in her calm words reached him. The hunter pulled up his net, gathered his scattered grain, and walked home with empty hands but a lighter heart. The dove fluttered back to her flock, and the forest breathed easier that day because one small voice had chosen kindness.

stories.title: The King Who Hushed the Night
stories.source: The Jataka · Vol. III, Lohakumbhi Jataka (No. 314) — E. B. Cowell ed., public domain
body: In the royal city, the king lay awake as terrible cries rose from the darkness. His family priest urged him to offer a blood sacrifice, insisting the omen would only be silenced by the spilling of a creature's life. The court murmured in fear, and the fires were almost kindled.

A young brahmin visiting the palace listened to the wailing and gently explained that the sounds were the lamentations of those who had already fallen into hell through their own cruelty. No beast slain upon an altar could quiet such grief, he said, for the cries arose from the long harvest of violence.

The king heard the truth in the brahmin's words and forbade the rite. Lifting his hand, he pledged to shield every living being within his realm, and from that night onward his people called him the protector of all creatures who walked the earth.

stories.title: The Doors That Opened for Mira
stories.source: Mirabai hagiographic tradition; see J. N. Bhatt, 'Meerabai' (Hindi), and Parita Mukta's English retelling, with reference to the Rajasthan and Vrindavan oral traditions
body: Mira, princess of Mewar, kept a small flame burning for Lord Krishna even after her royal in-laws forbade her from entering the temple. Night after night she sang her bhajans in solitude, refusing to let devotion be silenced by their command.

One morning the heavy temple doors swung open of their own accord, as if the shrine itself had been waiting for her. The family, witnessing what no power of theirs could explain, finally relented. Mira walked through the threshold with her lamp held high, her heart finally free.

Leaving Mewar behind, she traveled to Vrindavan, the land of her beloved Krishna. There she spent her remaining years composing hymns, serving pilgrims, and becoming the beloved saint-poet whose songs still warm the courts and villages of Rajasthan.

stories.title: Wings Over the Hundred Leagues
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana · Sundara Kanda, Sarga 60 (Gita Press translation)
body: The search parties of the vanaras had wandered to the edge of the world, their hearts grown quiet with despair at finding no trace of Sita. As hope thinned to almost nothing, an old feathered shadow settled among them on the rocks, Sampati, the elder brother of Jatayu who had long guarded those skies.

The grandsire vulture bowed his great head gently toward the weary young monkeys, offering the same selfless courage with which he had once shielded Jatayu from the burning sun. He stretched his vast wings, lifting himself above the sea so he might gaze across the full hundred leagues of ocean for them.

From his high perch Sampati spoke the word they had been longing to hear, pointing his curved beak toward the distant jeweled roofs of Lanka across the water, where Ravana kept Sita in captivity. The monkeys lifted their tired faces, and a small warm light returned to their expedition.
